title: High Court halts Kolkata civic polls until challenge to 209-ward map is decided
dek: A Division Bench barred the State Election Commission from calling KMC elections on the redrawn wards until the main petition is settled, making a December poll unlikely.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Calcutta High Court on Friday barred West Bengal's State Election Commission (SEC) from calling elections to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) on the basis of the redrawn 209-ward map until a court has decided whether the redrawing was lawful. The order is likely to push the city's civic polls past the December date the state government had been aiming for.

A Division Bench of Justices Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Arjun Ray Mukherjee, sitting as the High Court's vacation bench, partly allowed an appeal against a single judge's refusal to pause the process. The restraint will last "till disposal of WPA 31433 of 2026", the writ petition that challenges the state's 11 September notification increasing Kolkata's wards from 144 to 209, reports said. Kolkata has had no elected council since 8 June.

## What the court ordered

The bench restrained the SEC from issuing a notification calling KMC elections based on the amended Schedule II of the KMC Act, 1980, which lists the city's wards, according to reports. It modified the single judge's order of 29 October only on that point and left the rest of it in place. The bench said its observations were "tentative in nature insofar as final disposal of the writ is concerned", one report said, so the question of whether the new map is valid remains open.

The written order was not available on the High Court's website by Friday morning, and the reports did not set out the bench's full reasoning. At the hearing on Wednesday, the bench had observed, prima facie, that an elected corporation's powers could not simply pass to an Administrator. Because the KMC Act requires the state to act on the corporation's recommendation, it said, if the Administrator could make that recommendation "the State Government is giving an instruction to itself", one report said.

The order applies to the KMC. The reports did not say it covers the six other civic bodies, including the Howrah Municipal Corporation, that were expected to vote in the same first phase.

## The arguments

The appeal was brought by Dipu Das, a Kasba resident and former CPI(M) councillor, and argued by senior advocate Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya. He told the court that the new map was drawn on the recommendation of the KMC Administrator, Smita Pandey, who was appointed after the elected board was dissolved. As an employee of the corporation, he argued, she could not stand in for the elected body. He said the exercise amounted to gerrymandering, which the Supreme Court has held to be unconstitutional, and that ward boundaries were redrawn to benefit a particular party, reports said. The appeal also argued that the single judge had not considered large differences in the number of voters from one ward to another.

Advocate General Surajit Nath Mitra, for the state and the KMC, argued that the state could carry out delimitation even without a recommendation from an elected corporation, and that the Administrator held all the corporation's powers. He said the appeal was not maintainable because Das had not filed objections when the draft was published, and that the challenge had come late, since the notification was issued in September. He also relied on Article 243ZG of the Constitution, which bars courts from questioning laws on the delimitation of municipal wards and allows elections to be challenged only through an election petition after the vote. Das's side replied that the bar protects laws on delimitation, not actions taken under delegated powers, one report said.

## Background

The KMC's elected board was dissolved on 8 June and the corporation has since been run by an Administrator. The state invited objections to a draft schedule of wards on 5 August, the KMC (Amendment) Act, 2026 came into force on 20 August, objections were taken from 22 August to 3 September, and the final notification followed on 11 September, according to reports.

On 29 October, Justice Hiranmay Bhattacharyya refused to stay the new map. He found no prima facie case for interim relief and said the "balance of convenience and inconvenience is against passing of any interim order", because a stay would affect the public at large, one report said. He held that the Administrator was competent to recommend the change, and that Das could not object now after filing no objections to the draft. Das appealed, and on Wednesday, 4 November, the Division Bench reserved its order. It recorded that no election notification would be issued before Friday.

The timetable had already slipped. On Thursday the SEC postponed the final voter rolls for the KMC and six other civic bodies, which had been due on 12 November, without setting a new date. An SEC official told reporters that the final roll must be published seven days after the poll notification, and that under the circumstances elections could not be held before 30 November.

## What the parties have said

No party had commented on Friday's order by late morning. Their earlier positions are on record. In June, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said the KMC election would be held "by the first week of December", one report said. On Tuesday, in Siliguri, he said: "After Nandigram, Falta and Rejinagar, we will win Kolkata, Howrah and Siliguri in February," according to reports. Opposition parties, including the Congress and the CPI(M), have questioned the delimitation and booth maps. They have asked for the polls to be held only after the Election Commission of India publishes its revised voter rolls in January.

CPI(M) leader Kallol Majumdar had alleged that the BJP wanted to delay the polls because of disputes over candidates, a charge BJP leader Sisir Bajoria rejected. "We want elections on time," Bajoria told reporters, saying it was the opposition that was unprepared. A Trinamool district chairperson in south Kolkata, Ratna Sur, described election officials as "unprepared and clueless".

## What happens next

The challenge now goes back to the single judge for a final hearing. The reports differed on the timetable he set on 29 October. Two reports said the respondents have three weeks to file affidavits and the petitioner one week after that. Another reported four weeks for the state, two weeks for the petitioner, and a listing after six weeks. On either timetable, a decision before December looks unlikely.

That runs up against the law's requirement, noted in one report and by the single judge, that a dissolved corporation must be re-elected within six months, which for the KMC falls in early December. The state can challenge Friday's order in the Supreme Court. It had not said by Friday morning whether it would.

## Timeline

- 8 June: KMC's elected board dissolved; an Administrator takes charge
- 5 August: draft schedule of 209 wards published for objections
- 11 September: final delimitation notification issued
- 29 October: single judge refuses to stay the new map
- 4 November: Division Bench reserves its order and bars a poll notice until 6 November
- 5 November: SEC defers the final voter rolls for seven civic bodies
- 6 November: Division Bench bars a poll notice until the writ petition is decided
